Iran keeps finding gas. Getting it out is the problem. Iran has announced another major gas discovery, but with the world’s second-largest reserves already beneath its soil, Tehran’s problem is not finding gas but finding the money and technology to extract it.

Iran parliament advances controversial bill that could criminalize foreign contacts. Iran's parliament approved an amended section of a bill aimed at countering foreign influence on Tuesday, setting out definitions for foreign governments, foreign agents and a broad range of contacts with foreign entities, state media reported.

What Operation Economic Outcast means for Iran, and for everyone trading with. Washington has launched a global campaign to cut off Iran's remaining trade, and its central message is aimed at third countries: keep doing business with Tehran and lose access to the United States. Treasury is calling it an economic D-Day.

Pakistan, Oman mediation visits are White House deception operation – Kayhan. Recent visits to Tehran by regional mediators were part of a White House “deception operation,” the hardline Kayhan newspaper said on Wednesday, following separate visits by Pakistani Army Chief Asim Munir and Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi.

Family of detained British couple in Iran urges UK action after embassy return. The family of a British couple detained in Iran called on the UK government on Wednesday to arrange an urgent consular visit and medical checks, saying British diplomats had yet to see them since the embassy returned to the country last week.

Iran plotted to assassinate Netanyahu’s son in Florida – Newsmax. Iran allegedly plotted to assassinate Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s eldest son, Yair, while he was living in South Florida, Newsmax reported on Wednesday, citing a US law enforcement source familiar with the matter.

Iran fuel reserves may run dry within weeks, sources say. Iran's drawdown of strategic fuel reserves has reached a “red alert” level and could exhaust remaining stocks within weeks, fueling disagreement between President Masoud Pezeshkian and the Revolutionary Guards, informed sources told Iran International on Wednesday.

Will Mojtaba Khamenei's absence help the Islamic Republic survive?. Since Mojtaba Khamenei was named the Islamic Republic's third supreme leader, no one has seen him or heard his voice. That looks like weakness. It is worth asking whether it might instead be postponing the system's political death.

Iran flogs two women detained in January protests. Iranian authorities flogged two women detained during January’s protests 31 times each before transferring them to prison to serve custodial sentences, according to rights groups.

Tehran debates waiting out Trump’s economic war. As Washington intensifies its economic campaign, Iranian politicians and analysts are offering sharply different prescriptions for dealing with the United States: from resistance and phased negotiations to new trade routes or waiting Donald Trump out.

Iran sentences two more protesters to death as executions surge. Two more protesters detained during Iran’s nationwide demonstrations in January have been sentenced to death, US-based rights group HRANA reported, amid a rise in executions and capital sentences following the unrest.

Regional diplomacy tests path back to Iran-US talks. Regional diplomacy around Iran appears to be gathering pace, with Pakistan, Oman and potentially Qatar seeking to turn an emerging agreement over the Strait of Hormuz into a path back to negotiations between Tehran and Washington.

Trump says he is in no hurry for talks as Iran admits the strain. Iranian officials acknowledged mounting economic strain on Wednesday, and in the same breath restated their conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as Donald Trump said he was in no hurry to resume talks.

Canada says ex-Iranian official 'critical' to revenue tied to terror funding. A former senior Iranian official living in Toronto played a “critical” role in generating government revenue that helped fund Iran's military, weapons production and armed groups in the Middle East, Global News reported, citing Canadian government documents.

Who is Abolfazl Shekarchi, the Iranian general calling journalists military targets?. The Iranian general who has threatened Persian-language journalists abroad as potential military targets has a history of incendiary attacks on critics and was among officials who initially dismissed reports that Iran had shot down Flight PS752.

Iran's Bank Melli remains open in Germany despite sanctions. Bank Melli Iran's branch in Hamburg remains open despite EU sanctions that Germany says apply to the Iranian state-owned bank's German operation, as Washington steps up pressure for its foreign branches to be closed.

Man from Supreme Leader's empire takes the helm of Iran’s biggest online retailer. Two years ago the editor of Iran's most hardline newspaper said management of the country's biggest online retailer would "fortunately" pass to those who serve the state. It is now chaired by a former spokesman for the supreme leader's business empire.

Iran sentences woman detained during January protests to death. A court in Iran has sentenced Leila Abolhassani, a 43-year-old mother of two teenage daughters detained during the January protests in the central city of Shahin Shahr, to death on charges of “waging war against God,” a source familiar with her case told Iran International.

‘State-sponsored theft’: UN representative calls out rising seizures from Iran’s Bahá’ís. Iran’s rising wave of raids, arrests and property seizures against Bahá’ís amounts to “state-sponsored theft,” the Bahá’í International Community’s representative to the United Nations in Geneva said, citing hundreds of incidents since the January crackdown.

Three mediators in three days seek path back to Iran-US talks. Three regional mediators have visited Tehran in three days in an intensifying diplomatic push to revive Iran-US talks, even as the two sides remain deeply divided over the Strait of Hormuz and Washington’s economic pressure campaign.

Tehran debates austerity as US targets sanctions lifelines. As Washington targets the financial and trading networks Iran has used to withstand years of sanctions, economists and analysts in Tehran are debating how much more economic hardship the country can absorb to survive a prolonged economic war.

Iran threatens US economic interests if maritime blockade continues. Iran will target US economic interests if Washington maintains its maritime blockade, Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Thursday, as the Trump administration steps up efforts to tighten Iran’s economic isolation.

MTN : l’Afrique de l’Ouest, locomotive inattendue du géant sud-africain des télécoms. MTN affiche des résultats en forte hausse au premier semestre de 2026, portés par le rebond spectaculaire du Nigeria et la croissance soutenue du Ghana. L’Afrique de l’Ouest s’impose comme le nouveau moteur du géant télécoms sud-africain.

CEEAC : pourquoi le Centrafricain Jean-Jacques Demafouth fait son retour au Gabon. Jean-Jacques Demafouth rejoint la CEEAC comme conseiller diplomatique, fort de ses réseaux à Addis-Abeba et du soutien de Bangui. La mission de l’ancien ministre centrafricain est multiple.

TikTok, Facebook, X… D’Abidjan à Washington, une armée de cyberactivistes pro-Tidjane Thiam. Alors qu’en Côte d’Ivoire, le tribunal doit trancher le 22 octobre sur la destitution du président du PDCI, de nombreux militants, véritables soldats du numérique, le défendent sans relâche sur les réseaux sociaux. Une force d’influence qui est aussi très difficile à réguler pour le parti.

Comment Coris est devenu la première banque de l’UEMOA, aux côtés d’Ecobank. Pour la première fois depuis 2013, le groupe burkinabè d’Idrissa Nassa égale Ecobank avec 8,6 % des actifs. Derrière cette première place partagée, le secteur se recompose autour d’acteurs ancrés localement.

Au Cameroun, les déclarations du capitaine Effoudou vont-elles faire basculer l’affaire Martinez Zogo ?. Ex-agent du renseignement camerounais en exil, le capitaine Romuald Effoudou multiplie sur les réseaux sociaux les accusations contre Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh dans l’affaire Zogo. Peu de preuves, mais assez de bruit pour s’inviter dans le procès.

Tchad : reportage à Abéché, la plus soudanaise des villes tchadiennes. À moins de 200 km du Darfour, Abéché, la capitale du Ouaddaï, au Tchad, est au cœur de la crise soudanaise. Mais les liens, anciens, de la ville et de ses habitants avec le Soudan voisin sont éminemment politiques.

Santé de Paul Biya : comment le président camerounais a été remis sur pied. Paul Biya a enfin regagné le Cameroun le 20 août, tentant de faire taire les rumeurs sur son état de santé. Jeune Afrique révèle comment une double intervention, suisse et indienne, a permis sa récupération.

Côte d’Ivoire, Sénégal, Mali : les dessous des écarts de prix à la pompe. Fiscalité, subventions, plafonds : chaque État joue sa propre partition selon ses marges budgétaires. Sur fond de fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz qui fait flamber les prix à la pompe.

Mesfin Tasew, le discret gardien de l’empire Ethiopian Airlines. Arrivé par hasard dans le secteur aéronautique en 1984, Mesfin Tasew dirige Ethiopian Airlines, le premier transporteur africain. L’ingénieur en électronique vient d’être prolongé dans ses fonctions.

Côte d’Ivoire : comment Guillaume Soro tente de rester dans le jeu depuis son exil. Une rare vidéo de l’ancien Premier ministre, diffusée le 22 août, a relancé les interrogations au sujet de ses ambitions. Sans appareil politique autorisé en Côte d’Ivoire, où il est toujours condamné à la prison à perpétuité, il a néanmoins réorganisé son mouvement.

Maroc : ce que l’on sait de la dernière fuite « sécuritaire » de Jabaroot. Le groupe de hackers a revendiqué, ce 24 août, une nouvelle fuite de données présentée comme étant celles d’agents marocains de la sécurité et du renseignement. Selon nos informations, ces données ne proviennent toutefois pas d’un piratage des services de sécurité marocains.

Gazoduc Nigeria-Maroc : le mégachantier finira-t-il par voir le jour ?. Le gazoduc Nigeria-Maroc a franchi une étape décisive avec le feu vert de la Cedeao. Reste à financer et construire ce mégaprojet de 25 milliards de dollars, promis à un rôle clé dans l’approvisionnement énergétique européen.

Mama Omorou, l’ingénieur qui veut mettre l’école togolaise à l’heure des nouvelles technologies. Ingénieur discret sans passé politique, Mama Omorou va faire sa première rentrée en tant que ministre de l’Éducation nationale. Portrait de ce technicien à qui Faure Gnassingbé a demandé de réformer l’enseignement.

BOAD : pourquoi la reconduction de Serge Ekué est-elle bloquée ?. Alors que son mandat à la tête de la Banque ouest-africaine de développement s’achève à la fin du mois d’août, Serge Ekué n’a toujours pas été reconduit dans ses fonctions. Son renouvellement est paralysé par les tensions politiques au sein de l’UEMOA.

Cameroun : quand Ahidjo dénonçait Biya et son « régime policier de terreur ». Le 27 août 1983, le premier président du pays démissionnait de la direction de l’Union nationale du Cameroun, le parti unique. La dernière étape d’un divorce politique spectaculaire avec son successeur, Paul Biya.

Un an après le départ de Sidi Ould Tah, comment se porte la Badea ?. Sous l’égide de son président koweïtien, la Banque arabe pour le développement économique en Afrique entend poursuivre la transformation engagée ces dernières années. Mais les équilibres financiers et géopolitiques sont difficiles à tenir.

Au Maroc, la guerre des transfuges vire au bras de fer entre RNI et PAM. Cela fait des mois que la majorité menée par Aziz Akhannouch est traversée de tensions, mais un cap vient d’être franchi avec une attaque frontale du Rassemblement national des indépendants contre son allié, le Parti Authenticité et Modernité. Lequel n’a pas tardé à réagir.

Un proche d’Abdelmadjid Tebboune nommé à la tête de l’autorité algérienne de surveillance des élections. Depuis la fin de 2024, date du limogeage de son président, l’Autorité nationale indépendante des élections n’avait plus de patron en titre mais un simple intérimaire à sa tête. Une situation que l’opposition ne se privait pas de critiquer.

RDC : 10 choses à savoir sur Jean-Jacques Muyembe, le médecin toujours au front contre Ebola. Le gouvernement congolais s’appuie plus que jamais sur le virologue de 84 ans, codécouvreur du virus en 1976, pour mener une nouvelle bataille contre l’épisode de l’épidémie en cours.

Dangote, Vitol, Alpha MBM : qui remportera la bataille des raffineries en Afrique de l’Est ?. Trois géants de l’énergie se disputent le marché du raffinage en Afrique de l’Est. Derrière la course aux investissements, c’est le contrôle du brut, des infrastructures et des réseaux de distribution qui se joue.

Comment Sky Mali s’est engouffré dans le vide aérien laissé par Air France et Corsair. Le retrait de Corsair prive le Mali de son dernier lien aérien direct avec Paris. Sky Mali veut saisir cette occasion pour accélérer son expansion régionale et s’imposer comme un hub de correspondance vers l’Europe.

Élections locales au Sénégal : la Cour suprême maintient le flou sur la date des scrutins. Au Sénégal, la chambre administrative de la Cour suprême a rejeté les requêtes d’une partie de l’opposition et de la société civile, qui lui demandait de contraindre le président Bassirou Diomaye Faye à fixer la date des élections locales.

Pourquoi les négociations entre Patrick Vieira et la Fédération sénégalaise de football s’éternisent. Patrick Vieira n’a toujours pas signé son contrat de sélectionneur du Sénégal. Des détails restent à régler, dans un contexte tendu entre la fédération et Pape Thiaw, l’ancien coach de l’équipe.

Au Mali, comment Assimi Goïta tente de contenir le débat sur l’excision. Le débat a ressurgi à la faveur d’une campagne pro-excision sur les réseaux sociaux. La junte tente désormais de reprendre la main, donnant des gages aux religieux et demandant aux ONG de suspendre leurs actions de prévention.

Cameroun : imbroglio autour de la cession de Sosucam. Le changement de mains de la Société sucrière du Cameroun (Sosucam), qui doit quitter le giron de Castel pour être reprise par un consortium local, crée des remous. L’opération nourrit des crispations dans les rangs de la primature. Explications.

Football en Côte d’Ivoire : A’Salfo s’offre son club. Le ballon rond ivoirien est – aussi – une affaire de pouvoir et d’influence. Le leader de Magic System vient de racheter un club abidjanais. Il suit ainsi l’exemple de toute une série de ministres, de députés ou d’hommes d’affaires.

Entre Oligui Nguema et les Bongo, l’impitoyable traque des avoirs et des milliards. Depuis le putsch d’août 2023 au Gabon, le conflit opposant Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema à une partie de la famille de son prédécesseur, Ali Bongo Ondimba, ne cesse de s’envenimer. L’enjeu : un patrimoine colossal, que les seconds espèrent sauver de la traque lancée par le premier.

Cessions de Société générale en Afrique : pourquoi le processus s’enlise. En Afrique de l’Ouest et Afrique centrale, les ventes de certaines filiales du groupe français tardent à se conclure. Au Bénin, au Cameroun et au Togo, le désengagement du groupe français tourne au ralenti, entre blocages réglementaires et appétits souverainistes.

En Tunisie, les protestations contre « l’été de tous les délestages » prennent un tour politique. Si la Tunisie est habituée aux pénuries, l’été particulièrement caniculaire qu’elle vient de traverser a accentué les problèmes. Dans la rue et sur les réseaux sociaux, les citoyens accusent le pouvoir d’inaction. Le président, lui, évoque des actes de sabotage.

Dialogue national en RDC : Félix Tshisekedi exclut la participation du M23. En RDC, Félix Tshisekedi a annoncé l’ouverture d’un dialogue national « d’une durée maximale de trois mois », en excluant les rebelles de l’AFC/M23. Une porte reste cependant entrouverte aux combattants qui renonceraient individuellement à la lutte armée.

Le canal de Suez, chantier pharaonique et œuvre de la vie de Ferdinand de Lesseps, diplomate passionné et tenace. « Suez, canal historique » (2/6). Les tentatives de relier la Méditerranée à la mer Rouge se sont succédé depuis l’Antiquité. Mais il a fallu attendre l’entrée en scène de Ferdinand de Lesseps, pourtant ni scientifique ni ingénieur, pour que le projet se concrétise. Personnage haut en couleur, l’ancien consul du Caire a su mettre à profit son amitié avec le souverain égyptien, Saïd Pacha, pour financer et lancer les travaux.

Au Maroc, une grève des avocats longue de plus de cent jours paralyse la justice. L’Association des barreaux du Maroc proteste depuis le début de l’année contre une nouvelle loi régissant l’exercice du métier d’avocat. Elle voit dans ce texte une « atteinte à leur indépendance ».

Guinée : éboulement meurtrier d’une décharge à Conakry. La catastrophe, survenue après de fortes pluies, a fait au moins 31 morts et 22 blessés, selon le dernier bilan des autorités. Un précédent bilan annoncé par le gouvernement dimanche faisait état de 30 morts.

En RDC, la colère des soignants, en première ligne face à Ebola, mais rarement payés. Depuis début juillet, les agents de santé confrontés à l’épidémie multiplient les grèves sporadiques pour réclamer le paiement de leur salaire. Le gouvernement a reconnu des détournements de fonds qui fragilisent la riposte contre la maladie à virus Ebola.

Le premier âge du canal de Suez, à l’ombre des empires français et britannique. « Suez, canal historique » (3/6). De 1880 à 1914, l’Egypte a perçu moins de 1 % du chiffre d’affaires généré par la Compagnie universelle du canal maritime de Suez. Un revenu qui démontre la domination du Royaume-Uni et de la France sur la gestion de la voie d’eau au début du XXᵉ siècle.

Ayyoub Bouaddi s’engage à Manchester City, un transfert à l’étranger record pour un footballeur de Ligue 1. Le club anglais a officialisé, mercredi, le recrutement du milieu international marocain de 18 ans, en provenance de Lille, son club formateur, pour un montant estimé à 100 millions d’euros.

Au Maroc, les hackeurs du groupe Jabaroot publient les noms de 70 000 agents des services de sécurité et de renseignement. Une nouvelle fuite de données personnelles a été mise en ligne sur le réseau social Telegram, lundi 24 août. D’après les informations du « Monde », elle serait l’œuvre de cinq anciens agents de la direction générale de la surveillance du territoire exilés en Europe.

Centrafrique : ce qu’il faut savoir sur l’effondrement meurtrier d’une mine d’or artisanale. Au moins 100 personnes ont été tuées lors de l’effondrement d’une mine d’or artisanale, le 18 août 2026, en Centrafrique. Un drame qui relance le débat sur de la dangerosité de ces lieux d’extraction qui opèrent dans l’illégalité.

La guerre au Soudan, premier terrain du « pacte de La Mecque » entre l’Arabie saoudite, la Turquie et le Pakistan. Les trois Etats, soucieux de peser face à l’Iran et à l’alliance entre Israël et les Emirats arabes unis, soutiennent de plus en plus fortement les forces de Khartoum, en guerre contre les paramilitaires des Forces de soutien rapide. Riyad finance l’achat de matériel turc et pakistanais.

Mayotte : Sébastien Lecornu veut conditionner l’aide au développement pour les Comores à une meilleure collaboration dans la lutte contre l’immigration clandestine. En visite dans le département ultramarin, le premier ministre a annoncé mercredi un durcissement du dispositif de lutte contre l’immigration illégale avec davantage de moyens de surveillance et d’interception. Le gouvernement veut notamment renforcer la pression sur les pays d’origine et de transit des migrants.
En Algérie, douze morts dans des feux de forêt. Des dizaines de personnes ont été évacuées, les incendies progressant jusque dans des zones résidentielles de plusieurs régions du nord-est du pays.

Les enlèvements au Nigeria ont entraîné le paiement de près de 5 millions d’euros de rançon en un an. Au moins 7 825 personnes ont été kidnappées entre juillet 2025 et juin 2026, selon le cabinet SBM Intelligence, à Lagos, pour qui « l’enlèvement de masse est désormais la pratique dominante » des groupes djihadistes et des bandes criminelles.

A Mayotte, Sébastien Lecornu annonce des renforts humains et technologiques contre l’immigration clandestine. Le premier ministre, en visite sur l’archipel, souhaite aussi conditionner l’aide au développement fournie aux Comores et à six pays africains à leur coopération avec la France dans la lutte migratoire.

Ebola : des traitements et des vaccins à l’essai face à la pire épidémie de l’histoire de la RDC. Plus de 2 700 personnes sont mortes depuis la déclaration officielle de l’épidémie en République démocratique du Congo, mi-mai. Antiviraux, anticorps monoclonaux et vaccins : les organisations de santé sont lancées dans une course pour mettre au point des thérapeutiques.

Traverser le canal de Suez, un défi technique qui se paye en centaines de milliers de dollars. « Suez, canal historique » (4/6). L’axe reliant la Méditerranée à la mer Rouge est une artère essentielle du commerce mondial. Les navires qui l’empruntent – plus de 25 000 durant l’année 2022-2023, un record ! – doivent respecter une réglementation stricte et s’acquitter de droits de passage qui peuvent avoisiner 1 million de dollars.

« Face à Ebola, il faut multiplier les capacités actuelles de la riposte » : l’appel du directeur de l’OMS dans la lutte contre le virus Bundibugyo en RDC. Trois cadres d’organisations internationales de santé publique, dont le directeur de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, détaillent, dans une tribune au « Monde », les pistes à suivre pour enrayer l’épidémie qui se propage à grande vitesse en République démocratique du Congo.

L’Afrique, dernier rempart d’un Gianni Infantino contesté de toutes parts à la tête de la FIFA. Alors que les confédérations européenne, asiatique et nord-américaine ont demandé le départ du président de l’instance internationale du football, la confédération africaine se range derrière celui qui a largement choyé les pays du continent.

L’OMS déclare la fin de l’épidémie causée par le virus Ebola en Ouganda. En l’absence de nouvelle contamination recensée 42 jours après la sortie du dernier malade de l’hôpital, l’Organisation a déclaré la fin de l’épidémie en Ouganda. L’épidémie continue cependant de faire rage en République démocratique du Congo.

Le Cap-Vert, modèle africain en matière de soins maternels et infantiles : « Aucune femme qui attend un enfant ne peut dire qu’elle n’a pas pu être suivie ». Depuis son indépendance en 1975, l’archipel s’est progressivement doté d’un système de protection sociale efficace. La mortalité infantile y est l’une des plus faibles du continent.

Le canal de Suez, ou comment l’Egypte a fait d’un symbole d’exploitation l’instrument de son émancipation. « Suez, canal historique » (5/6). Un parfum de fronde imprègne l’axe maritime. C’est une révolte à Ismaïlia, l’une des villes du canal, qui a entraîné la fondation de la République égyptienne en 1952, mettant fin à une monarchie inféodée à Londres. Et c’est en nationalisant la voie d’eau, en 1956, et en la défendant contre les assauts français, britanniques et israéliens que le pays a construit sa légitimité internationale.

"The United States condemns the SAF’s recent air strikes inside Chad," Massad Boulos wrote on X of the Sudanese Armed Forces. "The violence must stop in Sudan and beyond. There is no military solution to this conflict—and absolutely no justification for expanding the violence beyond Sudan’s borders." Boulos said the SAF and the breakaway paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) "must immediately accept a humanitarian truce, protect civilians, and allow unhindered humanitarian access". He called on the United Nations Security Council, where the US wields veto power, to strengthen the arms embargo and sanctions packages. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Boulos demanded that "external financial and military support to the warring parties must stop", but he did not mention the United Arab Emirates or explain why the SAF would have bombed its African neighbor. The UN has said that the UAE routes weapons shipments to the RSF via Chad. Middle East Eye has revealed how Chad is central to the UAE's logistics network supplying the RSF. The Gulf state has played such an outsized role in prolonging the now three-year-long civil war that last year, Sudan's ambassador to the US, Mohamed Abdulla Idris, told reporters that his country would not accept any peace proposal that involves Abu Dhabi as a mediating party. "It's unacceptable to us," he said. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "The United Arab Emirates is a party to the conflict, so it cannot play both roles - become a party, and then become a mediator, no." Diplomacy The SAF said it was protecting its "sovereignty, security, and safety" when it struck a military convoy in Chad one week ago. A Chadian security source told the Reuters news agency that "the alert level has been raised to the maximum" as the country deployed 100 armoured vehicles and signal-jamming trucks to its eastern border with Sudan to ward off incoming drones. Statements like this do absolutely nothing to advance a diplomatic solution." Boulos promised a diplomatic solution in February, but it has not materialised. The US, he said, had readied the text of a peace plan for Sudan's civil war that included the approval of the members of the "Quad". The Quad, comprising the US, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Egypt, was formed to coordinate efforts to end the conflict in Sudan. The group initially unveiled a roadmap in September aimed at ending the fighting between the SAF and RSF. "We've been working on this comprehensive peace plan for at least three months now that should be acceptable to both sides," Boulos said at a fundraiser held to gather pledges for immediate humanitarian aid for Sudan. He indicated the text would be unveiled in mid-February. It never came. What he would not specify - despite being pressed by reporters - is exactly what, or who, is the obstacle to the plan's implementation, only saying that it is "quite comprehensive". Autopsy report reveals 5-year-old girl in Haripur was raped. HARIPUR: The post-mortem report of a five-year-old girl who went missing from outside her home in Haripur on Aug 10 and was later found dead revealed that she had been raped and died from excessive bleeding and shock, it emerged on Thursday. The child’s body was recovered from an unused well of a warehouse at about a furlong’s distance from her home on August 24 on the pointation of one of the four arrested suspects. According to the autopsy report, a copy of which is available with Dawn , confirmed that the minor was subjected to rape. Dr Munawar Afridi, who was part of the team that conducted the autopsy, told Dawn that the team had also collected body samples for DNA testing and forensic analysis and handed them over to the police for further proceedings. Separately, police confirmed to Dawn that the fourth suspect was produced before a magistrate today, who sent him on judicial remand. One of the members of the investigation team told Dawn that the suspect, a resident of the locality, had lured the child to follow him by asking if she wanted to see her father, who was waiting at a distance. District Police Officer (DPO) Shafiullah Gandapur told Dawn that he had requested the formation of a panel of prosecutors to examine the case and determine whether the anti-terrorism act could be invoked. He added that the four suspects were juveniles, hence “the situation called for strict adherence to legal provisions”. He further said that the police were still investigating the case. On Tuesday, speaking to the media at a press conference, Gandapur said the five-year-old went missing from outside her home at around 6pm on Aug 10. Police initially began an inquiry under Section 156(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), which deals with investigations into cognisable cases, and formally registered a first information report (FIR) under Section 364-A of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) relating to kidnapping or abduction with intent to murder, on Aug 12. The move followed the collection of CCTV footage and geofencing of the area, according to police. The DPO said police had initially arrested three suspects, one of whom recorded a confessional statement before a duty magistrate last week. According to the statement, four suspects were involved in abducting the five-year-old and taking her to an area near Model Town, where the suspect and another accused allegedly sexually assaulted her. According to Gandapur, none of the three suspects initially arrested by police disclosed where they had left the victim after the assault. However, during a search of the area, police obtained CCTV footage from another house, which helped them trace a fourth suspect. Acting on information provided by the fourth suspect, police recovered the five-year-old’s body from an unused well at a warehouse near one of the link roads leading to Haripur University, the DPO said. He said the suspect had thrown the child into the well after allegedly raping her and had attempted to conceal the body with foliage.

DPM Dar, British foreign secretary discuss Indus Waters Treaty, regional security: FO. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Thursday met British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, with the two discussing developments related to the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and the regional security situation, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The IWT has come under strain since India announced in 2025 that it was placing its treaty obligations in abeyance. The announcement followed an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam that killed 26 tourists — an incident New Delhi blamed on Islamabad without evidence. For its part, Pakistan strongly denied the allegations and called for a neutral investigation. In a post on X, the FO said DPM Dar, who is in the United Kingdom on a four-day official visit until Aug 28, highlighted India’s “persistent violations of its international obligations” and stressed the importance of upholding international law and treaty commitments during his meeting with the foreign secretary. The two met in London, where they held delegation-level talks, the FO said. It added that the two sides reviewed the “full spectrum” of Pakistan-UK bilateral relations. The two leaders also reached an agreement to establish a “structured mechanism for formal talks between the two foreign ministries to cover all areas of cooperation to further strengthen bilateral ties and regularly review progress in key areas”. “They underscored the importance of sustained high-level engagement and closer coordination on matters of mutual interest,” the statement added. It said the two ministers also discussed the situation in the Middle East, with DPM Dar highlighting Pakistan’s diplomatic and mediation efforts in the region and the progress achieved. Miliband, for his part, lauded Pakistan for its “constructive role and facilitation efforts in promoting dialogue, diplomacy and stability in the Middle East”. During the meeting, DPM Dar also raised alarm over the “terrorist threats emanating from Afghan soil”, in reference to threats posed by groups operating out of Afghanistan. “Both sides underscored the importance of sustained engagement in advancing peace, stability and cooperation in the region and beyond,” the FO said. It added that the two ministers also underscored the importance of the Pakistani diaspora in the UK, with a focus on “further strengthening the longstanding ties and people-to-people links between Pakistan and the UK”. DPM Dar has held a series of engagements over the past three days, including meeting the head of the International Maritime Organisation, where he had called for “urgent and effective institutional intervention” for the return of 10 Pakistani sailors held captive by Somali pirates. DPM Dar also interacted with British parliamentarians of Pakistani origin and met the Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey a day earlier.

Newborn left unclaimed at Pims for two months dies in blaze. ISLAMABAD: One of the 14 babies who died in Wednesday’s fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), Islamabad, was a two-month-old boy who had remained unclaimed at the hospital since birth. The infant had been living at Pims alongside other sick children. His body remains in the hospital mortuary following his death. He was born on June 21 to a young girl who appeared to be around 15 years old, said a female doctor at Pims who requested anonymity. The girl reportedly did not have documents to prove her marriage. The doctor told Dawn that hospital staff had asked “her husband and grandmother” to provide proof of marriage, but when they failed to produce the documents, “they left the baby and never returned”. The doctor said police had been involved in the case since the child’s birth and had refused to hand over the baby to the family until they provided proof of marriage. “The case was reported for medico-legal follow-up,” the doctor said. “It had been two months, and the baby was growing in the [Mother and Child Health (MCH)] nursery among sick babies,” she said. Another doctor told Dawn that the infant had been kept in an environment with a high risk of infection. “The child was also deprived of the necessary care essential for normal neurocognitive development. “Every child has a right to an identity, citizenship and a family in order to become a healthy member of society. That baby was fed and clothed through donations,” he added. He said all possible efforts had been made to facilitate the baby’s adoption, adding that the police had not followed up on the case in the two months since. The doctor told Dawn that, according to official hospital documents, the infant was listed as “baby of ‘H’, but we had named him ‘Ali’”. “Now, his dead body is in the mortuary. Only his legal heirs can receive the body,” he said. A woman places a flower outside the Mother and Child Health ward as she pays homage to infants killed in a fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) Hospital in Islamabad on August 27, 2026. —AFP Fire at Pims On Wednesday, 14 babies died after a fire erupted in the MCH ward at Pims. At the time, the health minister claimed that the fire began with a spark in the AC, while the bereaved families said the rescue teams arrived too late. According to a statement by the hospital, the incident was “initially caused by a spark inside nursery at 06:38am and within seconds a massive fire erupted due to oxygen points at each incubator”. It said two doctors and two nurses on duty inside the nursery responded “immediately and called security staff, who joined in and tried to get in twice [to bring] babies out until 06:39am, when a huge blast occurred and ceilings fell down”. Several witnesses, their hands and faces blackened from the smoke, told AFP they waited hours for help from the emergency services and were forced to smash through windows to get to the ward while some found the doors locked — an account the hospital and government later denied. Soon after the incident, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif formed an inquiry committee and removed federal Health Secretary Muhammad Aslam Ghauri. Meanwhile, a notification issued by the Islamabad district magistrate said that a seven-member fact-finding committee, headed by the additional deputy commissioner general (ADCG), had been formed to determine the facts behind the fire. Speaking to reporters in Islamabad on Wednesday, the health minister said he will present himself to his superiors for accountability. He said the incident was being investigated by “experts, different institutions including us”, adding that “nothing will remain hidden and all facts will be unearthed”. The incident has sparked outrage across the political spectrum, with many demanding accountability and criticising the hospital administration.

Pakistan questions Gaza ceasefire as killings of Palestinians continue. UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan has questioned how the Gaza ceasefire can be considered to be holding when Israeli strikes and civilian deaths continue, telling the UN Security Council (UNSC) on Wednesday that more than 1,200 Palestinians had been killed since the truce was announced. “If the ceasefire is holding — as we have been told — then how are strikes continuing and civilians being killed?” Pakistan’s permanent representative to the UN, Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, asked during a UNSC meeting on the situation in the Middle East. His remarks came amid growing concern at the UNSC that, despite the ceasefire and diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, conditions in Gaza remained dire and violence continued in both Gaza and the occupied West Bank. UN Acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov reported that Israeli airstrikes had resumed on Aug. 12 after a one-week lull. During the reporting period, he said, 100 Palestinians were killed and more than 400 injured. The humanitarian situation was also highlighted by Athena Rayburn, executive director of the Association of International Development Agencies, who said that improvements in aid delivery had not changed the broader reality facing Palestinians. “2 million Palestinians remain trapped and suffering severely,” she said. Against this backdrop, Pakistan also warned that Israel’s advancement of the E1 settlement project could further destroy prospects for a political settlement by effectively severing the occupied West Bank and threatening the territorial contiguity of a future Palestinian state. Ahmad described the project as a “dangerous escalation”, warning that it could put thousands of Palestinians at risk of forcible displacement. He noted that all members of the UNSC had rejected annexation and urged the UNSC to ensure that measures moving in that direction were stopped. Palestinian Permanent Observer Riyad H. Mansour went further, saying annexation had long been underway but that Israel had now “crossed the Rubicon” with the release of tenders for the E1 plan. “The Israeli government stated clearly that its goal in issuing these tenders was the destruction of the Palestinian State and the triumph of the settlers’ State,” Mansour said. He accused Israel of pursuing territorial expansion despite the consequences for regional peace. “They do not care that annexation kills any prospect for peace in our region,” he said, arguing that the destruction of the possibility of peace was itself part of Israel’s objective. The E1 project was one of several issues raised at the meeting as members and UN officials warned that developments on the ground were threatening diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. Several delegates condemned Israeli plans for 1,200 settlement units in the E1 area east of Jerusalem, saying the project could split the occupied West Bank and further undermine prospects for a viable Palestinian state. France, meanwhile, strongly condemned Israeli statements and policies concerning Gaza while stressing that the territory’s reconstruction and restoration of Palestinian institutions should not be made contingent on the completion of the disarmament process. French Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont specifically denounced remarks by Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir calling for Palestinians in Gaza to be killed each night. “We firmly condemn the public statements by the Israeli National Security Minister Ben Gvir, calling a few days ago for 30 or 40 people in Gaza to be killed each night,” Bonnafont said. He argued that the priority should be to restore basic living conditions and Palestinian governance in Gaza. “The restoration of decent living conditions cannot be subordinated to the finalisation of the disarmament process,” he said. France also called for an Israeli military withdrawal, with Bonnafont stressing: “It is important for the Israeli army to withdraw.” “Gaza and the West Bank are two integral parts of Palestine,” he added. The US, however, defended UNSC Resolution 2803 and President Donald Trump’s comprehensive Gaza plan, arguing that the arrangements offered an alternative to either continued Hamas rule or prolonged Israeli occupation. US Ambassador Michael G. Waltz acknowledged that Gaza continued to face serious humanitarian needs but pointed to improvements in aid access and nutrition as evidence of the impact of increased supplies reaching civilians. He also said Hamas had “twice committed to disarm”, arguing that reconstruction and an eventual Israeli withdrawal ultimately depended on the group relinquishing its military capabilities. The disagreement over sequencing — whether reconstruction and Israeli withdrawal should proceed alongside the disarmament process or depend on it — reflected a broader challenge facing the ceasefire arrangements. Speaking for the Arab Group, Qatari Ambassador Alya Ahmed Saif al-Thani stressed that an end to the Israeli occupation remained essential for any lasting settlement. “Just, comprehensive and durable peace cannot be achieved without ending Israeli occupation,” she said, while calling for Palestinians’ right to self-determination to be upheld. She also condemned what she described as “ongoing gross Israeli violations” throughout the Occupied Palestinian Territory and accused Israel of rejecting both the comprehensive peace plan and the goal of a Palestinian state. “This is a direct rejection of the Comprehensive Plan, jeopardising its implementation and fundamentally undermining collective efforts to achieve just and durable peace,” she said, urging its full implementation. UN officials and mediators also called for implementation of the 15-point Roadmap and Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. The plan envisages Hamas’s disarmament, an Israeli military withdrawal, an international stabilisation force and transitional Palestinian governance. Alakbarov and Nickolay Mladenov, High Representative for Gaza on the Board of Peace, urged the parties to implement the arrangements fully as the humanitarian crisis continued and settler violence persisted in the West Bank. Pakistan also called for the immediate release of Palestinian clearance revenues withheld by Israel, saying the funds were undermining the Palestinian Authority’s ability to provide essential services. Ahmad further condemned continuing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, citing UN figures showing about 190 attacks a month in early 2026 and calling for urgent international action to protect Palestinians. Pakistan reiterated its support for an independent Palestinian state on the pre-1967 borders, with Al Quds al Sharif as its capital.

Bangladesh to 'positively' consider joining Makkah pact if invited: foreign minister. Bangladesh would consider joining the Makkah Pact “positively” if invited by founding members, Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament on Thursday. “Joining the pact or not has not come yet, as it is subjected to the intention of the parties involved in the pact. If they invite Bangladesh to join, then we will definitely consider it positively,” the foreign minister said, assuring parliament that Dhaka would assess the potential benefits before making any decision to join. “More importantly, we have to keep in mind that it [the Makkah Pact] is the Muslim world’s self-defence mechanism,” he added. “And this is our family’s, the Muslim family’s, internal matter. So, there is nothing for others to be concerned about.” Separately, opposition leader and Bangladesh Jamaat-i-Islami Ameer (chief) Shafiqur Rahman said on Thursday that joining the Makkah Pact was Bangladesh’s “own decision.” “If Bangladesh takes a decision in the interests and needs of the country and nation, no one else needs to worry about it,” he said in a statement on Facebook. Earlier this week, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir said Dhaka had expressed interest in joining the pact. “If there is one [agreement] in West Asia, if there is a security agreement between Islamic countries, then it is not unusual to go there. Let’s see. The matter is being viewed positively,” said Kabir. ​​​​​​​Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the joint defence agreement at a trilateral summit in Makkah on August 7, pledging to strengthen collective security, deepen defence cooperation and promote peace and stability in the region and beyond. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement was signed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during the summit at Al-Safa Palace. The tripartite pact empowers member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them, and reflects their “shared commitment to further strengthening their collective security and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond, in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future”. Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had already signed the “ Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement ” in Riyadh last September, pledging that any attack on either nation would be treated as an act of aggression against both. In January, Reuters quoted Defence Production Minister Raza Hayat Harraj as saying that a draft had been prepared after 10 months of talks. Turkish FM Hakan Fidan had said Ankara favoured an “inclusive platform that creates wider, bigger cooperation and stability”. The pact has been welcomed by the United States, Bahrain and Somalia, with Turkiye expecting Egypt to join the pact “in the next stage”.

Punjab Assembly speaker stalls anti-terrorism amendment bill after opposition objections. LAHORE: Punjab Assembly Speaker Malik Muhammad Ahmad Khan deferred further proceedings on the Anti-Terrorism (Punjab Amendment) Bill 2026 after opposition lawmaker Rana Aftab Ahmad Khan objected to it on constitutional and procedural grounds, including the provincial legislature’s competence. Through the bill, the Punjab government has proposed sweeping changes to the anti-terrorism law that could allow terrorism cases to be tried under a highly confidential regime, including keeping the identities of judges, prosecutors, defence lawyers and witnesses secret. Raising his objections, PTI’s Rana Aftab termed the bill “unconstitutional” and demanded open and fair trials in terrorism cases. Meanwhile, Law Minister Rana Muhammad Iqbal maintained that the standing committee had discussed the bill threadbare and that the opposition should have raised its objections there. The Anti-Terrorism (Punjab Amendment) Bill 2026 The bill seeks to insert a new Section 21AAA into the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997, creating a “special security case” mechanism for cases in which participants are considered to require extraordinary protection. Under the proposed law, a designated authority — an officer of at least BS-20 whose identity would itself remain confidential — could declare a case or a class of cases a special security case. At the authority’s request, the chief justice of the Lahore High Court would assign the case to an Anti-Terrorism Court judge. The bill also proposes that the identities of judges, public prosecutors, defence counsel, police officers, witnesses and other persons involved in such proceedings “shall not be disclosed”. Judicial orders would carry official titles instead of the judges’ names, while witnesses would be identified through codes issued by the designated authority. The proceedings could be held at secure premises or conducted through video links, including from prisons. The proposed provision would also allow the government to adopt other security measures it considers appropriate. However, the proposed legislation has raised serious constitutional and judicial concerns, particularly over the transfer of powers traditionally exercised by courts to an executive authority. Aftab’s legal and constitutional note argues that the proposed system goes beyond witness protection and could create what amounts to “anonymous proceedings”. It points out that an accused person would not be able to challenge the constitution of the tribunal, seek the recusal of a judge or effectively question the judge’s independence if the judge’s identity remained concealed. The proposed sealed record has also been criticised as potentially undermining the right of appeal. Under the existing anti-terrorism act, the trial record is required to be transmitted to the high court, while the accused is entitled to a copy of the judgment. The note further argues that keeping the record sealed with both the chief justice and the designated authority could make appellate scrutiny difficult. The proposed provision also gives the designated authority a role in selecting prosecutors. The prosecutor general would provide a panel of five public prosecutors, from which the designated authority would assign one to the case. Another contentious provision allows the regime to be applied to a “class of cases”, rather than requiring a case-by-case judicial determination. The note argues that this could create a standing exception to open justice and leave considerable room for misuse because the bill does not clearly define what constitutes “extraordinary protection”. It also provides no specific mechanism for the accused to challenge the classification, no provision for periodic review and no sunset clause. The proposal has further been questioned on the grounds that existing law already provides several safeguards for threatened participants in terrorism cases. Section 21 of the ATA allows courts to hold proceedings in camera and restrict the publication of names of judges, prosecutors, counsel and witnesses. The Punjab Witness Protection Act 2018 also provides mechanisms for protecting witnesses and allows for proceedings through secure arrangements. The note maintains that the proposed law could therefore create an overlapping regime rather than filling a clearly identified legal gap. It also raises questions about the separation of judicial and executive powers under the Constitution, arguing that decisions concerning the conduct of trials, appointment of prosecutors and custody of judicial records should remain within the judicial framework and under the supervision of the high court. The bill’s “notwithstanding” clause, which gives the proposed provision effect over the Anti-Terrorism Act and the Code of Criminal Procedure, has also been flagged as a potential source of conflict with federal legislation and constitutional provisions. The proposed legislation comes amid security concerns surrounding judges, prosecutors, investigators and witnesses involved in terrorism cases. Its stated objective is to provide extraordinary protection to participants in such proceedings while maintaining fair-trial guarantees. The note, however, suggests that if the assembly intends to strengthen security arrangements, the bill should retain judicial control over the process. It recommends that the judge’s identity remain known to the parties and the appellate court, while witness anonymity should be allowed only through a reasoned judicial order. It further proposes deleting the provision allowing the mechanism to cover entire classes of cases and restricting the executive authority to recommending and arranging security rather than assigning prosecutors or issuing directions on how trials should be conducted. The note also calls for the trial record to remain available to the high court in usable form, judicial review of any special-security declaration and a sunset provision. At its core, the debate over the bill is whether enhanced security for those involved in terrorism cases can be achieved without compromising the constitutional guarantees of an independent judiciary, a fair trial and an effective appeal. The bill is aimed at protecting those at risk, but its proposed method of doing so — particularly the secrecy surrounding judges and the expanded role of an executive authority — is likely to become the central point of debate in the Punjab Assembly.

Smith and Cox revive England against Pakistan after Abbas strikes. Jamie Smith and Jordan Cox both scored fifties as England recovered from a top-order collapse against Pakistan to 248-9 when bad light ended Thursday’s opening day of the second Test at Lord’s. Veteran paceman Mohammad Abbas took three wickets for four runs in 16 balls, including the prize scalp of England captain Joe Root for just four, as the hosts slumped to 36-3 after Pakistan won the toss in helpful conditions for seam bowling. But Smith’s 61 and 55 from Cox — his second fifty in successive Test innings — got England back into the game and turned attention away from the late-night drinking incident that saw fast bowler Brydon Carse dropped from their squad. Abbas had fine figures of 4-56 in 15 overs and fellow seamer Mohammad Ali 3-67 in 17 when the umpires ruled it was unsafe to continue despite the floodlights illuminating the ground. Pakistan were woeful in all departments during an innings and 103-run defeat in the first of a three-Test series at Headingley last week. They did, however, have the worst of the conditions after losing the toss before being dismissed for meagre totals of 171 and 135. It was a different story in London, with Pakistan captain Babar Azam, the only change to either side as he returned from a finger injury in place of stand-in skipper Salman Ali Agha, opting to field on a green-tinged pitch under grey skies following a rain delay. Bails fly as Pakistan’s Mohammad Ali bowls out England’s Ollie Robinson for no runs on day one of the second test match between England and Pakistan at Lord’s cricket ground in London on August 27, 2026. — AFP Fine fielding Abbas, who has had stints with several English counties, was soon into his stride on a ground where he was named player of the match after taking eight wickets in Pakistan’s victory in their last Test at Lord’s in 2018. The 36-year-old was fortunate, however, when Emilio Gay glanced a legside ball only for diving wicket-keeper Mohammad Rizwan to hold an excellent one-handed catch. Ben Duckett fell for 17 when lbw to an Abbas nip-backer. Medium-pace bowling with the ’keeper standing up to the stumps has plagued England in recent times and Rizwan was up to the wicket when Abbas pinned Root on the back leg. Harry Brook was then bowled for 15 by a superb Ali delivery that jagged back, with England 80-4 at lunch. Dan Lawrence had made 10 when he flicked to midwicket, only for Shan Masood to drop a seemingly routine catch. Pakistan’s fielding was also poor as they tumbled to the bottom of the World Test Championship table with defeat in Leeds. But when Lawrence turned spinner Ali Usman legside and set off for a non-existent single, only to be sent back by Cox, he was run out by Masood’s accurate throw from mid-wicket to Rizwan. Cox, however, struck consecutive legside boundaries off Usman to complete an 88-ball fifty including seven fours. His partnership of 67 with Smith ended when substitute fielder Agha, belying Pakistan’s deserved reputation as a poor fielding side, held a superb slip catch off Khurram Shahzad. Smith, whose fifty came from a mere 63 balls, was clean bowled by Ali and two balls later the paceman dismissed tailender Ollie Robinson with another nip-backer. Jofra Archer launched Abbas for a straight six before the bowler had his revenge, with Gus Atkinson — who has a Test century at Lord’s to his credit — a useful 34 not out at stumps.

CDF Munir, Kuwaiti delegation vow to strengthen 'mutually beneficial defence partnership'. Pakistan and Kuwait reaffirmed the resolve to “consolidate their historic and brotherly relations into a strong, enduring and mutually beneficial defence partnership”, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Thursday. A Kuwaiti delegation led by Defence Minister Sheikh Abdullah Ali Abdullah Al-Saleem Al-Sabah met Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir at General Headquarters (GHQ) in Rawalpindi, ISPR said in a statement . The Kuwaiti minister was accompanied by Chief of General Staff of the Armed Forces Lt Gen Khaled Darj Saad Al-Shriaan. The two sides discussed “matters of mutual interest, regional security and bilateral defence cooperation”, ISPR said. “Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to enhancing institutional ties and expanding mutually beneficial defence collaboration between the two brotherly countries.” ISPR added that “the Kuwaiti delegation appreciated the professionalism, operational excellence and valuable contributions of the Pakistan Armed Forces towards regional peace and stability”. The two sides discussed contributing to regional security and stability as well. Pakistan and Kuwait also signed ‘Protocol Agreement 2026’, “significantly expanding bilateral military cooperation” under their 2023 Defence Cooperation Agreement, state-run Pakistan TV reported. The pact was signed during a meeting between the Kuwait defence minister and his Pakistani counterpart Khawaja Asif in Rawalpindi. “Pakistan’s Armed Forces will assist Kuwait in training, capacity building, border management and other mutually agreed areas of defence cooperation,” Pakistan TV added. The signing comes about a month after Kuwait ratified the 2023 agreement with Pakistan. Days after the ratification, Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah paid an official visit to Pakistan, where he met CDF Munir and discussed matters of mutual interest and regional security. Sheikh Jarrah had expressed appreciation for Pakistan’s steadfast support and constructive contribution toward regional peace and stability. During his visit, which was the first by a Kuwaiti foreign minister in more than five years, Sheikh Jarrah also called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and his Pakistani counterpart Ishaq Dar. There’s been a noticeable uptick in high-level contacts between the two countries over the past few mon­ths, including exchanges between senior military officials and discussions on expanding defence cooperation, as Kuwait broadened its security partnerships amid continuing volatility across the Gulf.

Trump orders Lake Ontario to be renamed 'Lake America'. US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that he is renaming Lake Ontario — a large body of water shared by the United States and Canada — “Lake America”. Trump signed an order in the White House in a move that comes amid a spiralling trade war between the world’s largest economy and its northern neighbour. “We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” the 80-year-old Republican told reporters in the Oval Office. “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people.” The name change — which Canada is unlikely to accept — mirrors Trump’s changing of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025. “The lake change, Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America,” Trump said. “So, if you think about it, we have a Gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.” In his inauguration speech last January, Trump said the Gulf of Mexico would be renamed the Gulf of America. A month later, Google changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America” for those using its Maps platform inside the United States, complying with an executive order by Trump. The tech giant wrote in a blog post that users outside the United States will continue to see both the original and new name for the Gulf of Mexico, as is the case for other disputed locations.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

JI announces nationwide strike on Sept 3 against petroleum levy. Jamaat-i-Islami Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Thursday announced a nationwide strike for Sept 3 against the petroleum levy , warning the government that if relief was not provided to the people, the ongoing sit-in campaign could culminate in a long march on Islamabad. “The rulers have neither a vision nor the ability to govern. Their only vision is to loot the people,” Rehman said while addressing participants of the JI sit-in outside the Punjab chief minister’s house in Lahore. He said the protest movement was no longer confined to three cities, with sit-ins and demonstrations now being held in several parts of the country. The party chief urged party workers and supporters to intensify their struggle, saying the government was testing the patience of the people. He also appealed to traders to support the Sept 3 nationwide strike in the interest of public rights. The JI chief said a major public gathering would be held in Faisalabad on Friday and indicated that the protest movement would be intensified in the coming days. Announcing the Sept 3 strike, Rehman said it would remain peaceful, stressing that “not even a flowerpot will be broken”. However, he warned that the government would have to accept the people’s demands. He said the JI’s campaign was not limited to the ongoing sit-ins but was part of a broader struggle against independent power producers (IPPs), the petroleum levy and the flour mafia. Rehman demanded the abolition of the petroleum levy and termination of what he called unjust IPP agreements . He also called for lower electricity and petrol prices for traders. He said the JI’s previous protests had secured relief for consumers in electricity prices and that the government must now provide similar relief on petroleum products. Turning to the Pims tragedy , the JI chief attributed the deaths of the children to government incompetence and negligence. He questioned how the government could run the country when it could not properly manage even a hospital. Rehman questioned why adequate safety measures had not been in place at Pims and whether doctors and paramedics had been properly trained to deal with emergencies and disasters. He said there was no effective system for disaster-response training in the country. He also questioned the formation of a committee by Pims after the prime minister had already constituted one to investigate the incident, saying the move appeared aimed at deflecting responsibility. He demanded a comprehensive investigation into the incident and said the matter could not be closed with the suspension of a single official. Rehman reiterated that the JI’s sit-in was aimed at securing the rights of Pakistan’s 250 million people. The state, he said, was responsible for providing basic rights to citizens, but successive governments had instead burdened them with taxes.

Pims starts referring serious gynae cases to Polyclinic, hospitals in Rawalpindi. • Holy Family Hospital receives eight patients as MS says no rush in gynae, paediatrics wards • BBH ready to cope with patients ISLAMABAD: Following the incident in which 14 newborn babies died , the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) has made temporary arrangements to refer serious gynaecological cases to Polyclinic and other hospitals in Rawalpindi. As many as seven gynaecological patients and a child were shifted from Pims to Holy Family Hospital (HFH). “We have a no-refusal policy, due to which all cases are accepted at the hospital. “However, as the nursery has been burnt and it will take some time to renovate and carry out repair work, it has been decided to refer very serious cases to other hospitals,” said a senior gynaecologist, who was not authorised to speak to the media. She said that even on Thursday, there had been three or four deliveries at Pims that could be considered serious, but the hospital realised that other hospitals could not take the load if Pims started referring every case. Newly-appointed Secretary Health Mohammad Mehmood, while talking to mediapersons, said that he had started efforts to bring in new technology to address the issues. “The infrastructure should be at an international level and governance should also be improved. I am new and do not understand the health sector, but my job is administration and I can do it. There are good and bad people in the hospital and they will give me suggestions. I have decided to sit in Pims so that I can understand the problems. I have additional charge of the health ministry and will try my best to address the issues,” he said. He said that he would run the ministry from Pims and remain at the hospital most of the time. When asked how it would be possible, Mr Mehmood said that it was the era of technology and everything was possible. “I can go out of Pims to attend important meetings, such as meetings chaired by the prime minister, but then again will come to Pims,” he said. Meanwhile, HFH Medical Superintendent Dr Ijaz Butt told Dawn that four female patients had been referred to the hospital by Pims management for treatment. He said there was no rush in the gynae and paediatrics wards of the hospital and they would manage the patients. He said the hospital had made special arrangements for the patients shifted from Pims and appointed an additional medical superintendent for coordination. He said the staff had been asked to admit patients coming from Pims. He said a special ward had been prepared to accommodate the patients, with doctors and nurses appointed to look after them. He said the hospital building had been constructed two years earlier and all the new equipment installed was in working condition. He said the latest mock exercise for fire safety was held on August 24 to train the staff by Rescue 1122. He said Wasa would install water hydrants at six points in the hospital, which had been lacking in the past. On the other hand, Benazir Bhutto Hospital (BBH) did not receive any patients. However, BBH Medical Superintendent Dr Sharjeel Sheikh told Dawn that a special desk had been formed to receive patients, but no patient had been referred so far. He said that for humanitarian purposes, he contacted the Dean of the Gynae and Paeds Department of Pims and asked them to shift the patients. He said the Pims administration thanked them and said it would send the patients. “We will deal only with emergency patients from Pims and in this regard, arrangements have been made in the emergency department,” he said. He said they had checked all the fire equipment in the hospital and found it to be in working condition. He said the hospital’s last mock exercise was held on August 8. Regarding water hydrants, he said Wasa had visited the hospital and recommended two points immediately and six more around the hospital in the coming days. Published in Dawn, August 28th, 2026

Hospital tragedy. WHERE does one begin? The mind goes first to the parents of the 14 newborns who died early Wednesday in the Mother and Child Health Ward of Islamabad’s Pims Hospital. The heart falters at the sheer scale of their loss. Their grief is shared across the country by people still struggling to comprehend how a tragedy of this magnitude was allowed to happen, and who must be held responsible. Multiple explanations have been offered for the fire: a short circuit, a spark, or an explosion involving an air-conditioning unit or its compressor. And every aspect of this incident unveils a new tragedy. Officials say the purified oxygen that should have been a lifeline for infants in respiratory distress instead accelerated the blaze dramatically. Within moments, the resulting inferno claimed the lives of 14 of the 15 babies in the ward. Eyewitnesses and parents described chaos: thick black smoke, shattered glass, locked or restricted doors, delayed rescue, and a near-total absence of proper evacuation protocols or functional fire-safety equipment. Some parents said they waited hours for help; official statements insisted fire tenders arrived within minutes of the emergency call. Rescue workers reported difficulty reaching the affected area. Hospital officials later acknowledged that the ward was routinely kept locked to prevent the theft of newborns. Clearly, there was no contingency plan for an emergency of this nature. And that, itself, is a damning indictment of the state of public hospitals. Equally frustrating has been the blame game that followed. Every stakeholder has been quick to point fingers even though few facts have been firmly established. The federal health secretary was swiftly suspended; scapegoated, many believe. But how far was he truly responsible? Is it fair, or even useful, to pin such disasters on individuals when the entire system remains broken? An inquiry committee has since been formed. That was necessary, and it is hoped that it will be able to diagnose the reasons that led to this tragedy. Yet, a much deeper reckoning is required. Removing a few officials will not prevent the next hospital fire. Pims is the largest and most prominent public hospital in the federal capital. It is the place where ordinary Pakistanis turn to in sickness, injury, and the hope of new life. Public hospitals in a country as populous as Pakistan need sustained resources and consistent support if they are to deliver even a basic standard of care and safety. Whether Pims ever received that support is a question that its administrators should be expected to answer. Until Pakistan stops chronically underspending on healthcare, the safety standards and quality of care in state-run hospitals cannot be expected to improve, and tragedies like this one will continue to claim lives. The bigger question is whether the authorities are ready to address that challenge. Published in Dawn, August 28th, 2026

Administrative delays aren’t employees’ fault, SC rules. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that the government, under the doctrine of good governance, had an executive responsibility to adhere to rules and regulations as employees could not be made victims or scapegoats because of administrative delays. “The employees cannot sit on [the] fence due to administrative or bureaucratic delays, inefficiencies, systemic delays, or in-house oversights or inadvertences of the departments as commanded by service laws jurisprudence,” observed Justice Muhammad Ali Mazhar. Justice Mazhar was heading a two-judge SC bench that took up service appeals filed by Sahibzada Hassan Ali and others against a Sept 12, 2025, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Service Tribunal decision denying seniority to regularised employees because of a belated official gazette notification. The SC, however, set aside the tribunal’s decision. ‘Model employer’ The 13-page judgement explained that the watchword “model employer” in administrative and service laws implied that the state and public authorities should act fairly and justly without exploiting technicalities. Court observes govt must follow rules and regulations, act as ‘model employer’ The controversy stemmed from the initial appointment of the petitioner employees against project posts through a June 30, 2016, notification under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Employees Regula­risation of Service Act, 2018. Their services were regularised through Aug 28, 2018, and Oct 17, 2018, notifications with effect from the Act’s commencement date of March 7, 2018. However, due to what the court termed the “lackadaisical attitude” (lack of interest) of the lower staff and the government’s Printing Press, the notifications were only published in the Official Gazette on Aug 21, 2024 — more than six years later. When the final seniority list for 2024 was issued, some employees filed departmental representations challenging the seniority of the petitioners. The KP Service Tribunal allowed these appeals, ruling that since the regularisation notifications were only published in 2024, the employees were not “regular civil servants” before that date and were thus not entitled to seniority. The SC considered whether on account of administrative lapses or unexplained delays, the employees should become victims or sufferers, notwithstanding that even in the delayed published notification, their date of regularisation was scribbled down as the effective date of the 2018 Act. “There is no such incidence put on view,” the judgement said, adding that since the regularisation was notified in the official gazette later, therefore, in the interregnum, the petitioners were sitting work-shy, inactive or at leisure without performing any duties or receiving remuneration in violation of doctrine of “no work no pay”. “There was no justification of how the respondents who were appointed much after the petitioners could claim seniority over and above the employees who were performing duties initially as project employees and were regularised subsequently by fiction of law,” the judgement observed. Clearing the air. THE morning after we landed in London three weeks ago, my nine-year-old and I went out for a walk post-breakfast. Out of nowhere, she said “Baba, I can breathe here.” I looked at her: she had a big smile on her face. She was not making a political or ideological statement; she was just making a statement of fact about the air. Living in Lahore, over the last two to three years we had gotten her used to wearing a mask all the time when outside. In London, I could see her face when we were walking that morning. I checked the Air Quality Index for London right after her remark: it was 20. I checked what the AQI in Lahore was at the time: it was 140. As I write this article, the AQI in London is 55 and around 150 in Lahore. The average AQI for Lahore last year was around 170. We had many days when the AQI was in the 200-300 range. For London, it was 42 in 2024 and 45 in 2025. Despite the fact that my daughter had to wear a mask whenever she was out in the open in Lahore, she still had to take medication containing montelukast sodium, which is commonly used for allergies and managing respiratory issues like asthma. It has been more of a friend to her over the last few years — a period in which she has been far sicker than in the first five to six years of her life — than any of her classmates. This was also the case with other children in her class and school. A paediatrician told me that children in Pakistan seemed to be living on this particular medicine — at least much more than on chocolates or other sweets. School absences on account of sickness have risen as well. We have yet to see a major sustained effort to reduce air pollution in the country. There is no dearth of evidence regarding the deleterious impact of air pollution on human health. In children, lung development as well as brain and cognitive development, are impacted. In adults, sustained exposure to air pollution increases the risk of heart disease, blood pressure, strokes, dementia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other respiratory issues. In some places, hospitals gear up for surges in the number of patients coming in with specific complaints (heart attacks in the elderly, etc) if the air quality is poor and has been poor for some time. Long-term exposure to air pollution has a significant impact on the health and longevity of all, but it has a more serious impact on children as their capacities are still developing. London had come a long way from the days of the London smog. But it was still not enough. So, in 2019, despite widespread scepticism and stiff opposition from many quarters, the mayor of London sanctioned the implementation of the Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) programme. It was eventually expanded to all London boroughs. Under the programme, vehicles had to meet stricter emission guidelines or pay stiff fines. Since it raised costs for vehicle users and owners, it was not popular but a recent five-year study has shown the significant impact it has had on children’s health. According to the study, ULEZ is strongly associated with accelerated and restored lung function growth in children. The study compared children in London with children in Luton. Both had comparable air quality rules to start with, but Luton did not come under ULEZ. At the start of the study, London’s children had significantly smaller lungs than their peers in Luton. But over five years, children in London caught up with those in Luton and the proportion of children with clinically impaired lung function dropped by five per cent. A separate study showed that over 2019-2024, deaths linked to toxic air fell by about 40pc alongside a 41pc drop in nitrogen dioxide in London. Scepticism about ULEZ has gone down. There are a number of British cities that are now implementing or contemplating the implementation of similar programmes. The mayor of London recently said that the implementation of ULEZ was the hardest decision he had to make as mayor but the results have shown it was needed and that the children of London were reaping the rewards now. Heating systems in Sofia — the capital of Bulgaria — were very dependent on coal and wood burning. These are being replaced as part of a citywide clean air programme, which includes a subsidy for low-income groups. Results already show an approximately 20pc reduction in the emission of harmful particulates. It is not just cities in rich countries that have done this or are doing it. London, Paris and Barcelona may be good examples of what can be done in just a few years, but it is cities in the not-so-rich countries that are also cleaning up the air or have plans to do so, because the cost of inaction is far too high. Bogotá — the capital of Colombia — is doing more work in this area. It has cut air pollution by about 24pc since 2018. The Kenyan capital of Nairobi passed an air quality law in 2022 that commits to cutting harmful emission by half by 2035. Hundreds of cities are embarking on the journey to clean up the environment. There is a lot of discussion of these issues in Pakistan whenever we have a season of high AQI numbers and schools are closed and emergency action is taken to address pollution. But we have not seen major medium- to long-term initiatives to take us to a place where the lungs and brains are not impacted by pollutants in the air, and where medication is not our children’s best friend. Though resolute and comprehensive action requires significant state buy-in and commitment, we also need a lot of citizen action to motivate and push the state. On both fronts, we need much more work and attention. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
