Qatari PM holds Tehran talks. DUBAI: The prime minister of Qatar visited Tehran on Thursday in a bid to revive diplomatic channels, as the US and Iran traded recriminations over Washington’s latest sanctions drive, described by one Iranian official as “all-out economic war”. Qatar has served as a back-channel negotiator for the warring parties and played a direct role in securing a June ceasefire that briefly led to a cessation of hostilities. Qatari PM Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who is also his country’s foreign minister, held talks in Tehran with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. The two discussed a proposed phased framework that includes establishing a temporary joint Iranian-Omani shipping corridor through the strait and carrying out a joint project to clear mines from the waterway, Qatar’s foreign ministry said. The two officials also reviewed the latest developments in the region and efforts to de-escalate tensions and create conditions for dialogue, the Qatari ministry said. The visit came even as the White House maintained there were currently no negotiations happening between the US and Iran, as Tehran had not yet “come to the table in a meaningful way”. Iran has repeatedly said it has never left the negotiating table. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said on Thursday that President Donald Trump “continues to retain all options on the table” with regard to Iran. Meanwhile, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf called on Thursday for national unity in the face of what he described as “all-out economic war”, warning that internal division was “exactly what the enemy wants”. Ebrahim Azizi, the head of the Iranian parliament’s national security committee, said the sanctions were an “inhumane and hostile act” which nonetheless had lost their effectiveness. Tehran has lived under various forms of US sanctions since the Islamic revolution in 1979. On Wednesday, the IRGC said that Iran and Oman had agreed on how to share the Strait of Hormuz and its revenues, but a senior Iranian source later said the two countries were still working on the details of an agreement. Published in Dawn, August 28th, 2026

PML-N fields ‘fresh face’ for AJK PM election today. MUZAFFARABAD: The Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Legisl­ative Assembly is set to elect a new prime minister today (Friday), with the dominant PML-N fielding a relatively young leader for the coveted office. The decision to nominate Barrister Syed Iftikhar Ali Gillani was announced by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif at a meeting with four senior PML-N leaders from AJK in Islamabad, late on Wednesday night. The meeting, which took place at the Prime Min­ister’s House, was attended by PML-N AJK President Shah Ghulam Qadir, his predecessor and former AJK premier Raja Farooq Haider, the party’s regional secretary general and asse­mbly speaker, Chaudhry Tariq Farooq, and Deputy Spe­a­ker Ahmed Raza Qadri. The prime minister was accompanied by his aide, Rana Sanaullah, and senior PML-N leader Saad Rafique. Mr Gillani was also invited to PM House but did not join the meeting, where PM Shehbaz infor­med the visiting leaders that party supremo Nawaz Sharif had decided to nominate him as the party’s candidate for the AJK premiership. The decision, however, triggered a sharp reaction from Mr Qadir and Mr Haider, who reportedly expressed their disagreement and announced that they would not participate in Friday’s election process. Speculation that Mr Gillani could be chosen for the premiership had been rife since he was elected to the assembly on a reserved seat on Aug 24. However, the party’s regional leadership believed that the formula followed in 2016, when Mr Haider was elevated as prime minister, would be repeated this time as well. Following the reaction of the two senior leaders, Mr Sanaullah and Mr Rafique held another meeting with them, but it remained inconclusive, sources told Dawn. In a post-midnight message on X, Mr Qadir assured the “self-respecting people of Azad Kashmir” that he would not compromise on their honour and dignity. “Nawaz Sharif’s slogan of giving respect to the vote will be ensured,” he added. On Thursday afternoon, however, PML-N central information secretary and Punjab senior minister Marriyum Aurangzeb posted on X that Mr Sharif had finalised Mr Gillani as the party’s candidate and directed him to submit his nomination papers for election as AJK prime minister. He will face PPP’s Sardar Mukhtar Ahmed Abbasi in Friday’s election. The AJK Assembly comprises 53 members, but its present strength is 46 because elections to seven seats in Poonch and Sudhnoti districts have yet to be held. The PML-N currently has a strength of 32, including its allies, while the PPP has 14 lawmakers in the AJK Assembly. According to Assembly Secretary Amjed Latif Abbasi, nomination papers would be submitted between 9:30am and 10:30am, followed by scrutiny at 10:45am and display of the list of contesting candidates at 11am. Candidates would be allowed to withdraw their nominations until 11:30am, after which the final list would be displayed at noon. The assembly will convene at 2pm for the election. Members wishing to vote for a particular candidate would proceed in single file through the entrance to the designated lobby of that candidate, where tellers would record their division numbers. The speaker will then count the votes cast through the division process and declare as prime minister the candidate securing the required majority. Meanwhile, preparations for Mr Gillani’s oath-taking ceremony have also been revised. Though Mr Qadir had tasked the administration with making arrangements at the High Court ground, the ceremony will now be held at the President’s House between 4pm and 5pm. Human Rights Watch slams ‘ruthless’ Taliban govt after ban on protest. KABUL: Human Rights Watch slammed on Thu­rsday the “ruthless effort to suppress all dissent” by the Taliban government, after a new police law banned demonstrations across Afghanistan. The 84-page legislation published by the justice ministry outlines a series of changes to law enforcement nationwide, including the rule that “all types of protests are banned”. Elaine Pearson, Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said the measure is “another step in the Taliban’s ruthless effort to suppress all dissent”. “The Taliban authorities fear any dissent and so they are escalating their repression,” she said in a statement. The Afghan government did not respond to requests for comment on protests being outlawed through the legislation, which was made public this month. Demonstrations have been rare during the Taliban administration’s five years in power. At least two people were killed in June when security forces allegedly opened fire at a women’s rights protest in Herat, a group of UN experts said. Amnesty International described the police law as “another sweeping assault on human rights in Afghanistan”, with the protest ban “among its most egregious provisions”. A polity or petri dish?. CONTRARY to the interior minister’s recent claim , bad governance is not the cause of the recurring collapse of political systems. It is only a symptom of a deeper systemic malaise — an undemocratic dispensation that allows the rulers to escape political and institutional accountability for their ills and excesses. The minister’s panacea for bad governance — the creation of more provinces — is also misconceived, if not potentially disastrous for a country already riddled with multiple fault lines. Enforcing central authority over multiple sub-national units has become increasingly difficult for authoritarian states or contested governments. Nigeria, Afghanistan, Sudan, Libya, Syria, Yemen, Iraq and Somalia are some of the many countries that have a large number of provinces; yet they are perennially afflicted with bad governance, fractious territories, economic meltdowns, civil wars, armed insurgencies and institutional breakdowns. The genesis of our systemic maladies can also be traced to a combination of undemocratic and authoritarian models that have been tried for decades on various pretexts — ideology, faith, stability, security, integrity, development, etc — to elude a legitimate federal democracy. Therefore, the answer to key political questions regarding the state’s foundational objectives, system of governance, people’s rights and liberties, and the distribution of resources within the federation and among the people has never been attempted. These are basic questions that the first generation of a political leadership must respond to, by way of a social compact that secures legitimacy, recognition, order and cohesion for the newborn state. Else, these questions hover over regicide, fratricide and every revolt or revolution. The common thread running through all successful social compacts is the ‘will of the people’. The people are the bedrock of modern states. They constitute the foundation of the state and work and sustain it with their blood and sweat. No polity can stand, let alone perform, without the people as the object and drivers of state-building. But it is unfortunate that right after independence, a small coterie of elites — political, business, landed and the civil-military establishment — captured power and diverted resources towards their own political and institutional interests. Constitution-making remained stalled for many years. And then in 1954, a mentally incapacitated governor-general dissolved the first elected constituent assembly, which had just finished the draft of the constitution, because he feared losing his arbitrary powers. The common man has borne the crushing burden of failed experiments. The constitution that was finally enforced in 1956 was neither democratic nor federal. It artificially created a ‘parity’ between the numerically divergent eastern and western wings of the country, denying the Bengalis their democratic right to rule based on the principle of majoritarianism. It also arbitrarily erased the western wing’s ethno-cultural diversity by forging a single province (One Unit), to weaken federalism. But neither scheme worked. The ensuing political instability and palace intrigues toppled as many as five governments in just two-and-a-half years, making it easier for a scheming and ambitious president to fold up the entire system, putting the country under the first martial law in 1958. The second exercise in political engineering was no less disastrous. The 1962 constitution was conceived by Gen Ayub Khan. He was ably assisted, among others, by a bevy of ambitious technocrats and unscrupulous judges. Retaining the ill-conceived One Unit and parity, he introduced a presidential system that denied universal adult franchise and sought ‘legitimacy’ from local governments — the basic democrats — which being malleable elected him and his loyalists to the federal and provincial legislatures. Interestingly, believing that it went against the ‘genius’ of the people, he dispensed with parliamentary democracy — something that India had successfully instituted years before in 1950. No wonder, the so-called ‘decade of development’ sowed most of the ills that continue to bedevil the political system to this day in the form of authoritarian masquerades, judicial kowtowing, electoral manipulation, ineffectual legislatures, crony capitalism, feudal empowerment, war-mongering, class inequalities, and the erstwhile east-west disparity. And small wonder that the sham democracy collapsed when protests swept the country in 1969 — another martial law was enforced, civil war broke out and half the country seceded in 1971. The 1973 Constitution — the third, in 26 years — has been the only compact that nearly reflected the ‘will of the people’, though it was framed by a post-1971 ‘rump’ parliament. The Constitution was almost consensual because the political leadership enjoyed a considerable degree of latitude in the post-1971 interregnum when the security establishment lay low. As a result, the Constitution cured much of the earlier ills, providing a fairly workable federal democracy. It included a parliamentary form of governance, a trichotomous balance of power, incremental autonomy for the provinces, fundamental rights and a fair amount of judicial independence. Above all, it recognised the people as the ultimate repository of political power and ‘trustees’ of sovereign authority. Thus, a solid foundation was laid for an institutional democracy. Had it been allowed to flourish, the country would have had a mature, stable and rules-based democratic order. But it was not to be. The elder Bhutto’s authoritarian streak, the opposition’s myopic vision and combative style, and a resurgent security establishment waiting in the wings, collectively brought down the constitutional dispensation in just four years. In 1977, the country again saw martial law. This time, the dictator sent an elected prime minister to the gallows. Since then, the polity has been turned into a petri dish of political engineering, a kaleidoscopic permutation of polities — naked martial laws, rule by a ‘troika’, ‘controlled’ democracy, imported rulers, dummy governments, a ‘hybrid’ model, and so on. Ironically, all these failed experiments were billed as ‘solutions’ to systemic problems. In reality, they were organised ‘institutional’ attempts to thwart constitutional democracy. All along, vested interests thrived, while the common man bore the crushing burden of failed experiments. But alas, the polity is back on the petri dish. The proposed scheme of creating more provinces on the pretext of addressing ‘bad governance’ is another experiment to dodge legitimate constitutional governance. It is bound to fail being superimposed, fanciful and unmanageably disruptive. The solution lies in a federal democracy — that is the only system that can ensure good governance and devolution to the third tier of governance. IHC reserves verdict on pleas for Imran-style facilities. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Thursday reserved its verdict on petitions seeking treatment at private hospitals and communication with relatives through WhatsApp calls for three prisoners of Adiala jail, observing that prisoners’ rights could not be ignored merely because they were behind bars. Justice Muhammad Asif reser­ved the judgement after hearing arguments from the petitioners, Advocate General Islamabad Naveed Hayat Malik, Advocate General Punjab Barrister Zafarullah and jail authorities. The petitions were filed by Adiala jail prisoners Owais Altaf, Ilyas Khan and Muhammad Ismail. The pleas seek permission for treatment at private hospitals as the necessary medical facilities are allegedly unavailable at government hospitals, as well as permission to communicate with relatives through WhatsApp calls. The matter has assumed significance following the Supreme Court’s Aug 18 order directing authorities to shift PTI founder Imran Khan to a private hospital for medical examination and treatment. Three other Adiala prisoners subsequently approached the IHC seeking similar relief. During Thursday’s hearing, the petitioners’ counsel argued that one of the prisoners was suffering from a serious bleeding disorder and had developed internal bleeding in the large intestine, which could prove life-threatening. The counsel said the prisoner had been in jail for around six months and had repeatedly been taken to hospital for treatment. He argued that if the required treatment was not available with­­in the prison or government hospital system, the prisoner should be shifted to a private hospital. He further contended that the SC order was still operative and that its directions could not be treated as applicable only to the PTI founder. The lawyer argued that prisoners were also citizens and were entitled to equal treatment before the law. “Why can the relief given by the Supreme Court not be extended to a common prisoner?” the counsel questioned. According to arguments, one of the petitioners, Muhammad Ismail, is an undertrial prisoner who has remained incarcerated for around six months and is suffering from a heart ailment. The lawyer alleged that the Superintendent Adiala jail had rejected the request for treatment without consulting a doctor. Barrister Zafarullah maintained that the authorities would follow whatever was provided under the law and prison rules. The judge observed that the petitions involved two distinct issues. On the issue of treatment, the Punjab law officer opposed the requests for shifting the three prisoners to private hospitals. Justice Asif, however, cautioned that the authorities could not “play with the illness of a prisoner”. The court also examined the request for communication with relatives through WhatsApp. Justice Asif questioned where the law prohibited a prisoner from speaking to his family. The Punjab Advocate General replied that the rules permitted calls to persons residing in Pakistan, adding that exceptional circumstances could be considered if a disease could not be treated at a government hospital. Gilgit-Baltistan to auction 117 trophy hunting permits. • Base rates set at $200,000 for markhor, $25,000 for blue sheep and $11,000 for ibex • Open auction scheduled for Sept 10 in Gilgit GILGIT: Gilgit-Baltistan’s Parks and Wildlife Department will auction hunting permits for three Astore markhors, 14 blue sheep and 100 ibexes for the GB Trophy Hunting programme 2026-27. The highest permit base rate is for markhor, set at $200,000. The base rate for blue sheep hunting permits has been set at $25,000, and at $11,000 for Himalayan ibex. The auction notice said that out of the exportable quota of four Astore markhors, one permit had been extended from the last hunting season, so three new permits would be auctioned in September. The open bidding for the permits will be held on September 10 at the Forest Complex in Jutial, Gilgit. According to the official notice, trophy hunting will be conducted under GB Trophy Hunting Guidelines 2019 from October 15 to April 10, 2027. Hunting would be permissible only in the designated conservation areas. The trophy hunting quota had been set on the basis of annual surveys conducted by wildlife experts, the notice said. GB Chief Conservator Parks and Wildlife Zakir Hussain told Dawn that last year, Rs350 million was collected from the auctioned permits against a target of Rs550m. He added that permits for two Astore markhors, five blue sheep and 10 exportable Himalayan ibexes went unused in the 2025-26 trophy hunting programme, resulting in a loss of Rs200m. Mr Hussain had told Dawn at the time that the law and order situation following violent protests in Gilgit and Skardu — against the assassination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei — had led to the cancellation of hunting plans by American and other foreign hunters. Business owners and tour operators have been opposing the permit rate hikes for the past two years, claiming that the decision had damaged their businesses. They have warned of losses for businesses and the local communities who rely on trophy-hunting revenue. Ikram Beg, a business owner who sells hunting equipment, said the trophy hunting conservation programme in GB was facing a serious challenge. “Over the last two years, the Wildlife Department has repeatedly increased trophy hunting baseline price by more than 300 per cent without adequately considering the recommendations of key stakeholders,” he said. Published in Dawn, August 28th, 2026

Infant deaths at Pims prompt Sindh govt to renew fire safety directives. • PMA warns health facilities in the province remain vulnerable to fires; urges concrete steps to improve safety measures for patients and staff • Chief Secy orders review of fire safety measures at all public places, buildings • KMC, SESSI-run hospitals told to ensure installation of extinguishers, alarm and fire detection systems KARACHI: The tragic loss of 14 infants in a fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) in the heart of the federal capital has also brought to light the highly risky conditions prevailing at health facilities across Sindh, prompting authorities to issue directives to review and strengthen fire safety measures at all health facilities, public places and buildings. The issue was also taken up by the Pakistan Medical Association (PMA), whose representatives warned at a press conference on Thursday that health facilities in Sindh were no less vulnerable to such an incident, while calling for concrete steps to make hospitals safe for both staff and patients. Thursday also saw a high-level meeting chaired by Sindh Chief Secretary Asif Hyder Shah, who issued directives to all provincial departments to complete reviews of fire safety arrangements at all public places, buildings and institutions under their administrative control and submit signed compliance certificates within 15 days. ‘A predictable outcome of criminal negligence’ Speaking at the press conference, PMA’s Dr Abdul Ghafoor Shoro said the fire at Pims was a predictable outcome of criminal negligence, complete administrative breakdown and structural failure. “If a flagship institution operating directly under federal oversight lacks functional emergency exits, maintained fire suppression systems and basic safety protocols, we must confront an uncomfortable truth: our healthcare system is in crisis from the top down,” he said. Pointing to the state of health facilities in Sindh’s rural and underprivileged areas, he said their conditions were far worse. “Millions of vulnerable citizens are forced to seek care in dangerous, crumbling facilities that lack basic fire protection, functional equipment and physical security for patients and medical staff alike.” Recalling some fire incidents at Sindh’s hospitals — the National Institute of Child Health (June 2026), Syed Abdullah Shah Institute of Medical Sciences (November 2025) and Sindh Government Hospital Liaquatabad (February 2024) — that resulted in the death of four health staffers, the PMA representative emphasised that these tragedies indicated structural failures across the country’s healthcare system. “Hospitals must be sanctuaries of healing — not places where infants and patients pay for administrative failure with their lives,” he said. The association demanded immediate resignation and removal of the entire Pims executive administration and the senior officials directly tasked with facility management and regulatory oversight. It also called for an immediate, third-party safety and security audit of every public and private healthcare facility across Pakistan, prioritising high-risk rural and district hospitals, and Rs100m compensation to each aggrieved family. ‘Over 3,300 buildings audited for fire safety in Sindh’ At the meeting chaired by the CS, Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) officials said that a total of 3,354 buildings had been identified and audited for fire safety across the province. They said 798 buildings were inspected in Karachi Division, 1,287 in Hyderabad Division, 420 in Larkana Division, 129 in Mirpurkhas Division, 418 in Shaheed Benazirabad Division and 302 in Sukkur Division. Referring to past fire incidents, the chief secretary said that timely safety measures, trained staff and well-organised evacuation plans could significantly reduce loss of life and property. “Fire safety is an ongoing responsibility and cannot be limited to a one-time inspection,” he said. The CS directed all administrative departments and divisional commissioners to ensure full compliance in every facility, with special priority for public places, government buildings, commercial centres, shopping malls, markets, prisons, hospitals, teaching hospitals, industrial facilities, schools, colleges, hostels, child protection institutions, Dar-ul-Amans, orphanages and bus terminals. He said special safety measures and workable emergency evacuation arrangements must be ensured in institutions housing children, women, patients, students, prisoners and other vulnerable groups. Healthcare body to conduct surprise inspection The Sindh Health Care Commission (SHCC) has directed healthcare establishments across the province to ensure full compliance with the commission’s prescribed standards for fire safety, emergency preparedness and disaster readiness. “The SHCC will now conduct surprise inspections and monitoring visits across Sindh, without prior notification, to assess the actual level of compliance with the prescribed safety standards,” a spokesperson of the commission said. During these visits, he added, SHCC inspection teams would not only physically assess fire safety and emergency arrangements but would also verify relevant records and documentary evidence. KMC, SESSI intensify fire safety measures at hospitals The Karachi Metropolitan Corporation and the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution (SESSI) have also issued fire safety directives to all health facilities operating under their administrative control. The KMC directed heads of all its health facilities to review and strengthen the fire safety measures; ensure installation and availability of adequate fire extinguishers at all appropriate and easily accessible locations, including wards, operation theatres, laboratory, store, kitchens, electric rooms and other high-risk areas. The hospitals were asked to ensure installation and functional maintenance of fire alarm and detection systems, provision and maintenance of clearly marked and unobstructed emergency fire exits with appropriate lighting and display of emergency evacuation plans and fire safety instructions at prominent locations for the guidance of patients, attendants and hospital staff. Also, SESSI Commissioner Hadi Bakhsh Kalhoro directed the relevant authorities to inspect fire alarms, fire extinguishers and emergency evacuation routes in all hospitals. They told me to remove my uterus. I refused.. Remove your uterus; it’s the simplest solution. My gynaecologist pronounced the verdict just months after I had my first miscarriage, hardly a year into my marriage. I remember sitting across from her with my arms wrapped around my abdomen, where the pain was the worst—it felt like someone had kicked me hard in the stomach. I was diagnosed with submucosal fibroids at the age of 26. It is a non-cancerous tumour that grows in the muscle just beneath the inner lining of the uterus and is common in about 25 per cent of women between the ages of 18 and 45 across the world. Think of it this way: the uterus is like an onion, made up of several layers. Submucosal fibroids grow on the layer nearest to the centre of the uterus, where a baby would develop. Irrespective of their position, fibroids cause heavy periods. During the first few days, particularly, the pain is so severe that it is impossible to move. At night, I lay paralysed in bed for hours, praying for an end to the misery. In the morning, painkillers—as many as four—helped me function, barely. My periods have always been this painful. But why they have always been this way is something I found out on the first scan of my very first pregnancy, which was terminated a month before my second trimester ended. Four months later, I was in the boxy clinic of my gynaecologist, where she told me the ‘only solution’ that exists for my condition. Removing the uterus will cure it, she said, almost as a matter of fact, as if the organ my body was built around was disposable. I refused. Thus began a 10-year journey that took me from one doctor to another and ultimately to an alternative most women never knew about: a procedure that could treat what was wrong with me without taking my uterus. But reaching there meant going through two rough pregnancies. During my second pregnancy, a majority of the doctors I met were very direct: get your uterus removed without trying to conceive ever again. I held my ground, and thankfully found a doctor who was eager to support me in those nine anaemic months. I had to undergo four follow-up scans every month to track the baby’s growth and position, not to mention the several times I stayed the night at the hospital for pre-term labour pain, triggered by the growth of the baby, and the fibroids. The cycle repeated six years later. At the time of my third delivery, I had around five to six fibroids covering nearly the entire outline of my uterus—it was truly a miracle that my baby survived. That was the point where my husband and I made the reluctant decision not to have more children. By this time, my doctors too had warned that I would need a myomectomy sooner or later. It is a generally recommended procedure to remove fibroids, which often converts into a hysterectomy—in which both the uterus and fibroids are removed—due to medical complications such as excessive blood loss. I wasn’t a stranger to the procedure. I had watched my mother go through multiple surgeries for fibroid removal, all of which ultimately led to a hysterectomy. After that, I saw a real decline in her health, and that of several other women her age who went through the same. It was for this reason that I had decided against it and that I had realised the uterus was not just a reproductive organ. So my quest for better treatment continued. I had grown more desperate than ever. After my last pregnancy, things took a serious turn: my period got so heavy I couldn’t step out of the house. I used that time for obsessive research, and that’s when I came across Uterine Artery Embolisation —a procedure that shrinks fibroids by blocking the blood vessels that feed them. The procedure itself follows a set sequence: a sedative and IV line to keep the patient comfortable, local anaesthesia at the groin, a small incision to reach the femoral artery, and a catheter guided by X-ray up to the uterine arteries. Dye is injected so the doctor can see the vessels feeding the fibroids, then tiny particles are released through the catheter to block that blood supply. Once the fibroids are cut off from circulation, the catheter is withdrawn and pressure is applied to the incision to stop the bleeding. In comparison with a hysterectomy or a myomectomy, the recovery tends to be faster. There’s no major incision, hospital stays are shorter, and the uterus stays where it is. A 2025 study by Dr Ziauddin Hospital in Karachi—which followed 67 women treated for symptomatic fibroids—found that patients were typically discharged within hours, if not days, and that those who responded to treatment saw symptoms improve within one to two days. In my case, the stay was two and a half days, followed by counselling for post-op pelvic pain, which took a week to subside. Just like every other procedure, this treatment too comes with risks: abnormal bleeding, uterine infection, internal injuries, blood clots, and a small chance of premature menopause in women over 45. Some also go through post-embolisation syndrome in the days following the surgery, which involves pelvic cramps, low-grade fever, nausea and fatigue that typically lasts between two and seven days and can easily be managed with medication. Since I had done my research, I knew what to expect and managed it with medication. And yes, since the procedure does not involve removing the uterus, pregnancy remains possible. However, there isn’t enough research on that front yet. That said, as successful as it is, the procedure is not cheap. It generally runs between Rs400,000 to Rs1,000,000—at least twice the price of a myomectomy or hysterectomy. Yet, for a majority of the women I met during my journey, money was never the deciding factor, autonomy over their bodies was. Hence the question arises: why don’t women know about the treatment? Part of the answer is structural. The procedure is performed by interventional radiologists and technologists, not gynaecologists. Research on the question backs this too: even as favourable outcome data for the treatment grew, many gynaecologists still did not routinely offer it as an alternative to hysterectomy or myomectomy, and patients seeking less invasive options sometimes had to bypass their gynaecologist altogether, going directly to an interventional radiologist themselves or getting referred by a primary care doctor. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists gives Uterine Artery Embolisation a Level-A recommendation as a legitimate alternative for women who want to keep their uterus. Yet, hysterectomy remains what one industry publication called the “gold standard from payers’ perspectives”, largely because it is a one-time, definitive procedure that’s simpler for insurers to process than an evolving, sometimes-repeated embolisation course. None of this involves a doctor telling a patient her uterus is good for nothing. It points to a referral gap built into the way medicine is structured and paid for. The fix then is awareness, not blame. Years back, when my gynaecologist told me to get my uterus removed, I had said no because I was educated and stubborn enough to keep asking the same question: is there any other way to treat this condition? But not every woman walking into a clinic today has the means, the confidence, or the information to do the same. That’s the gap I am trying to close. Please consult a qualified doctor to confirm your diagnosis before considering any treatment, including Uterine Artery Embolisation.

Trump administration seeks to restrict internships for international students. US President Donald Trump’s administration has issued a memo for ​universities, seeking to restrict the issuance of certain internship work authorisations for international students as the federal government ‌warns that colleges not complying with the regulations may lose certification to enroll foreign students. The federal memo dated August 24 said the Student and Exchange Visitor Programme (SEVP), which is part of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), has “observed a rise in Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorisations that appear to ​violate regulatory requirements which permit CPT only where the training is an integral part of an established curriculum”. “Failure to ​comply with SEVP regulations may result in an institution losing certification to enrol foreign students,” the ⁠memo said. It resulted in some schools, including the University of California, Los Angeles and the University of California, Berkeley, pausing certain ​applications for work authorisations for international students. “UCLA has paused certain Curricular Practical Training authorisations while it reviews recent federal guidance and determines ​next steps,” a UCLA spokesperson said. UC Berkeley’s international office said the August 24 memo was “more narrow in focus, more direct, and includes content that is more restrictive in nature”. The federal government had also issued an earlier memo in mid-August. UC Berkeley’s international office said it is unlikely that it ​will process certain work authorisation applications “in the near future” and urged those international students to plan accordingly. It said it will continue ​processing “degree-requirement” CPT as normal and would resume processing “Doctoral Dissertation and Master’s Thesis Research CPT”. The office said it would consult legal experts to develop ‌new processes ⁠aligning with new federal requirements. “Nothing about these regulations has changed,” the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent, said in a statement. “However, schools and employers should consider themselves on notice: under President Trump, abuse of this generous system will no longer be tolerated.” Trump has targeted universities with probes and funding threats over issues like pro-Palestinian protests against US ally Israel’s assault on Gaza, diversity initiatives, climate ​programmes and transgender policies. Rights ​advocates have raised free speech, ⁠academic freedom and due process concerns. Separately, the US Justice Department (DOJ) alleged on Thursday that admissions practices at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Services favoured Black and Hispanic applicants, citing ​findings of a probe as the Trump administration continued its diversity crackdown. “We are disappointed by the ​DOJ’s conclusions, which ⁠we believe are incorrect,” the university said, saying the admissions policies were in compliance with law and not discriminatory. The Justice Department has alleged similar bias at other schools, saying the department aims for settlement talks. If those efforts fail, the department will file suit, it ⁠said.

PM Shehbaz says Makkah defence pact has sent 'message of peace, unity throughout region'. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday said that the recent Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan had brought the three countries “closer together” and sent a message of “unity and peace throughout the region”. ​​​​​​​The three countries signed the joint defence agreement at a trilateral summit in Makkah on August 7, pledging to strengthen collective security, deepen defence cooperation and promote peace and stability in the region and beyond. According to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), PM Shehbaz made the remarks during a meeting with Saudi Minister for Environment, Water and Agriculture Abdulrahman bin Abdulmohsen Al-Fadley at the Prime Minister’s House in Islamabad. In a statement, the PMO said the premier reaffirmed the “deep-rooted, fraternal ties” between the two countries and conveyed his regards for King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud. He underscored that as strategic partners, both Pakistan and the kingdom must now focus their energies towards “deepening economic and agriculture ties to translate their longstanding relationship into a stronger, mutually beneficial trade and investment partnership”. PM Shehbaz also expressed satisfaction at the “constructive engagement” between the two sides, particularly with regard to the export of agricultural products by Pakistan to the kingdom, the statement said. “Both sides also exchanged views on enhancing agricultural productivity in Pakistan, through the use of technology, research and development and more efficient use of water resources,” the statement added. The premier also announced that a delegation of agricultural experts from Pakistan would soon visit Riyadh to carry forward these discussions “with a view to realise the full potential of this partnership”. Meanwhile, the Saudi minister thanked PM Shehbaz for the warm hospitality extended to him and his delegation and reaffirmed the kingdom’s commitment to deepening cooperation with Pakistan across the agriculture, water and food security sectors, the statement concluded. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement was signed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif during a summit at Al-Safa Palace. The tripartite pact empowers member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them, and reflects their “shared commitment to further strengthening their collective security and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond, in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future”. Pakistan has said that the pact is “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles. On Thursday, Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said the country would consider joining the pact “positively” if invited by the founding members.

Two days on, rescuers scour debris in Nepal as risk of fresh flooding grows. Rescue teams on Friday used heavy machinery to dig through mud and debris in Nepalese towns devastated by a flash flood two days ago, as hopes of finding survivors faded and officials worked to reduce the risk of further catastrophic flooding. The confirmed death toll in Nepal rose to 469 people early on Friday, with almost 1,000 more missing there and in neighbouring Tibet, near where a glacier collapse on Wednesday morning sent a huge torrent of rock, ice, mud and debris cascading through Himalayan mountain river systems. The flood ripped through villages and valleys, destroying power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. Of those missing, at least 540 are foreigners. Authorities in Nepal used helicopters to search for survivors and drop emergency supplies to thousands cut off in towns and valleys while emergency services, some using sniffer dogs, recovered dozens of bodies swept down into the plains. Rescuer help women to move through a muddy road following flash floods and a mudslide in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal on August 28, 2026. —Reuters Dibga Tamang was among the last people rescued from the hard-hit town of Rasuwa on Thursday, airlifted along with three others to an army camp in Nuwakot. “All of our people have gone. They are dead,” Tamang said. “I have no one left waiting for me. Everything and everyone is gone. The end.” The sheer amount of water and debris stirred up now risks triggering a further disaster. Nepal’s disaster management authority warned that a lake formed by debris blocking the Bhotekoshi River was rising and at risk of bursting, while on the other side of the border China said that some three million cubic metres of water, the equivalent of about 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools, was expected to flow into an already dammed lake over the next three days. There is a high risk the lake could breach, with peak flow expected around September 1, Chinese state media said, citing the water resources ministry. Chinese authorities have mobilised an eight-member engineering team to conduct aerial surveys and 3D modelling of the barrier lake, but accessing it was challenging. “After the glacier collapse created the lake, many isolated cliffs and steep cliffs appeared along it,” one of the engineers, Chen Hanxiao, told CCTV. Chen said the general approach to reducing the lake’s threat is to excavate a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, but the width and depth of that channel needed calculations based on how fast the water will flow and how quickly the lake will fill. Their next tasks were to monitor the lake and collect data from the lake floor, as well as weather monitoring in the coming days. Torrent tore through border crossing Chinese rescuers had yet to reach the worst-hit area on the Chinese side of the border, the Gyirong border crossing, by Thursday evening, state media reports indicated, as crews worked to clear debris from the key access road leading to the area. Dramatic footage on Wednesday showed enormous torrents of muddy water and debris tearing through structures in the border crossing area within seconds and engulfing people trying to flee. An excavator in action as rescue workers repair a road leading to Gyirong Port after a mudslide, in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China on August 28, 2026. —Reuters The tally of missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County was 558, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday, including 260 foreign nationals. So far, just three people have been confirmed dead on the Chinese side. China’s Premier Li Qiang arrived at the disaster-stricken site in Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, state-run Xinhua news agency said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority. Buildings ‘wiped out like toothpicks’ Around the world, relatives of those missing were desperate for information about their whereabouts. Sneha Sudhir was one of 10 women whose husbands had set out from Nepal on a trek to Tibet’s Mount Kailash when the region was struck by disaster. The men, all from northern Virginia, are among dozens of Americans missing. “Where are they?” Sudhir said tearfully from her home in Chantilly, Virginia, on Thursday. Sudhir said the women were supporting each other and reaching out to officials, politicians and friends and family in the United States and India, hoping for word. “Everybody is taking turns in shedding their tears, wiping it off and getting back to work,” she said. US President Donald Trump said America had offered support to Nepal. Rescued residents react as they meet family members at an army camp following flash floods, in Battar Bazar town of Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 28, 2026. —AFP “Nobody’s ever seen anything quite like that, where very powerful, strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks. It’s a terrible thing. We are sending aid and we’ve spoken to the leadership and we let them know anything they want, they’ll have.” Ganesh Aryal, the administrator of Chitwan district, said authorities had recovered 103 bodies from the river system in his district, which is about 100 kilometres away in the plains from the worst-hit region of Trishuli. With local hospitals unable to accommodate all the bodies, district authorities were setting up tents and making arrangements for families to claim their dead relatives, he said. Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who visited flood-hit Nuwakot on Thursday, said the situation was still difficult. “All the state agencies are operating at full capacity. Our first priority now is to save the life of each citizen, search and rescue of the missing, treat the injured and provide immediate relief to the affected families,” he said. Reintegration program continues for Manila shelter kids. The Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW) on Thursday, Aug. 27, continued its “Kaagapay Mo sa Buhay” reintegration program, assisting children from the Reception Action Center (RAC) and the Manila Boystown Complex in reuniting with their families and communities. Under the program, District Welfare Offices will provide assistance and conduct follow‑up monitoring as children return to family care. The effort aims to support their transition and help them rebuild their lives. The program also includes livelihood aid to strengthen families during reintegration and improve living conditions. The “Kaagapay Mo sa Buhay” program is a weekly event organized by the city’s social welfare department for children apprehended for curfew violations. According to MDSW, children will remain under the custody of RAC for a week after being taken in. Those who remain unclaimed by a parent or guardian after the one‑week period will be transferred to the Manila Boystown Complex in Marikina. Authorities will then conduct profile verification for children who remain in temporary care to trace their families or guardians. (Shane Quiachon)

Man arrested for stealing cop's car radiator in QC. Police arrested a 41-year-old man for allegedly stealing a car radiator worth P3,500 from the vehicle of a police officer in Barangay Maharlika, Quezon City, on Wednesday, Aug. 26. The suspect, identified only as alias “JM,” allegedly took the radiator from a vehicle parked outside an automotive service establishment on Mayon Street at around 9:20 p.m. Police said the victim, a police officer, had brought his vehicle to the establishment for repair due to a defective radiator. While the vehicle was being serviced, the victim temporarily placed the radiator on the cemented pavement outside the establishment before briefly going inside. When he returned, he discovered that the radiator was missing. The victim immediately sought assistance from personnel of the La Loma Police Station (PS 1), who were conducting patrol operations in the area. The responding officers and the victim conducted a roving search in the vicinity, which led to the arrest of the suspect and recovery of the stolen radiator from his possession. Police records showed that the suspect had a previous case for an alleged violation of Republic Act No. 10591, or the Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act, in June 2024, and cases involving Presidential Decree No. 1602 (illegal gambling), Republic Act No. 10591 (firearms law), and City Ordinance No. 5121 (anti-deadly weapons measure) in April 2018. The suspect is facing a theft charge before the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office.

KATSEYE cancels Daisy Chain Fields appearance after Megan suffers injury. Another setback has hit KATSEYE, with the global girl group pulling out of Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival after Megan Skiendiel suffered an ankle injury during a tour rehearsal. KATSEYE announced through Weverse that it would no longer perform at the women-led music festival, scheduled for Aug. 29 at Great Park in Irvine, California. The group said Megan sprained her ankle during rehearsal and, after being evaluated by doctors, was advised to stay off it and allow it to properly heal ahead of KATSEYE’s upcoming tour. “Megan sprained her ankle yesterday during tour rehearsal and after being evaluated by doctors, she has been advised to stay off it and allow it to properly heal so we can be ready for our upcoming tour,” the group said. The members apologized to fans who had been looking forward to seeing them at the festival. “We know how much our fans were looking forward to seeing us and it breaks our hearts to disappoint anyone who made plans to be there,” KATSEYE said. The group said it was particularly excited about Daisy Chain Fields because of its focus on music, joy and community. “We were especially excited for Daisy Chain Fields because it’s not just about music, but the greater mission of joy and community,” they added. KATSEYE also sent its support to Rodrigo and the other performers, nonprofit organizations and volunteers involved in the event. “We’re sending all our love to Olivia and to all of the incredible artists, non-profit organizations and volunteers who have given their time to make this day so special,” the group said. “We’re sending all our love to Olivia and to all of the incredible artists, non-profit organizations and volunteers who have given their time to make this day so special,” the group said. Following KATSEYE’s withdrawal, Devon Again was added to the festival lineup. Megan’s injury comes at a difficult time for KATSEYE, which has already been navigating activities with a reduced lineup. The group has continued performing without leader Sophia Laforteza, who announced earlier this month that she was taking a temporary hiatus to prioritize her mental health and well-being. Her return will be reassessed in September. Sophia’s hiatus came months after Manon Bannerman also stepped away from group activities to focus on her health and well-being. Before Megan’s injury, KATSEYE had been performing as a quartet consisting of Daniela Avanzini, Lara Raj, Megan and Yoonchae Jeung.

Parañaque cops seize loaded gun from construction worker. A construction worker was arrested after police found a loaded .38-caliber revolver during a search operation in Parañaque City on Thursday, Aug. 27. Police said the suspect, identified as Edwin, 39, of Hontiveros Compound, Barangay San Antonio, was arrested at around 5:10 p.m. Members of the Parañaque City Police Station Intelligence Section served the search warrant issued by Judge Moises D. De Castro of the Parañaque Metropolitan Trial Court. The operation resulted in the recovery of a .38-caliber revolver loaded with four live rounds of ammunition.
